name: Charlemagne
info: Charlemagne (748–814) was King of the Franks from 768, King of the Lombards from 774 and emperor from 800, who united most of Western and Central Europe and was crowned in Rome by Pope Leo III.

facts.born: 2 April, most likely in 748 (an older tradition gives 742); place unknown; eldest son of Pepin the Short and Bertrada of Laon, of the Frankish Carolingian dynasty
facts.died: 28 January 814, after seven days bedridden with pleurisy; buried that day in the palace chapel at Aachen
facts.role: King of the Franks (768–814, jointly with his brother Carloman I until 771); King of the Lombards (774–814); emperor (800–814)
facts.known: uniting most of Western and Central Europe; the conquest of the Lombard kingdom, Bavaria and Saxony; his coronation as emperor by Pope Leo III in 800; the Massacre of Verden and the forced conversion of the Saxons; the Carolingian Renaissance; reforms of administration, law, coinage and the church

t: Charlemagne succeeded to the Frankish kingdom with his brother in 768, became sole king in 771, and by conquest added the Lombard kingdom, Bavaria and Saxony to his rule.
His wars against the Saxons lasted over 30 years and included the beheading of a recorded 4,500 prisoners at Verden, laws punishing pagan practices with death, enslavement and forced removals.
Crowned emperor in Rome on Christmas Day 800, he ruled from Aachen, legislated on government, church and learning, and was later claimed as a predecessor by both French and German monarchs.
dyk: As an early sign of friendship Charlemagne asked the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid for an elephant; the animal, named Abul-Abbas, arrived at Aachen in 802.
ev: Born, most likely in April of this year, the eldest son of Pepin the Short and Bertrada of Laon
Succeeds his father as king of the Franks with his brother Carloman and is crowned at Noyon
Carloman dies suddenly, leaving Charlemagne sole king of the Franks
Pavia surrenders; Charlemagne deposes Desiderius and takes the title of King of the Lombards
After Widukind defeats a Frankish army, has 4,500 Saxon prisoners beheaded at Verden, as the annals record
Pope Leo III proclaims him emperor and crowns him at mass in St. Peter's Basilica on Christmas Day
Crowns his only surviving son, Louis, as co-emperor at an assembly at Aachen
Dies of pleurisy and is buried in the chapel at Aachen

sections.early:
Charlemagne was born into the Carolingian family, which had risen as mayors of the palace under the Merovingian kings of the Franks. His grandfather Charles Martel, after whom he was named, left the throne vacant from 737 and planned the division of the kingdom between his sons Carloman and Pepin the Short, who succeeded him in 741. In 744 Pepin married Bertrada, a member of an influential noble family; Charlemagne was their eldest son.

His year of birth is uncertain. An older tradition, resting on his biographer Einhard, the Royal Frankish Annals and his original epitaph, gives 742. Karl Ferdinand Werner challenged this from an annal recording the birth in 747, and Matthias Becher showed that 2 April, the day commemorated at Lorsch Abbey, would have fallen in 748, since the annalists began the year at Easter; most scholars now accept April 748. The place is unknown.

His native tongue was a Germanic language, and he was probably bilingual in Germanic and Romance dialects from an early age; he also spoke Latin. The extent of his formal education is unknown, though he was almost certainly trained in military matters at his father's itinerant court. Whether he could read is debated: Johannes Fried thinks it likely, while Paul Dutton concludes that he probably never properly mastered the skill. By 751 or 752 Pepin had deposed the Merovingian Childeric III and replaced him as king. In 754 Pope Stephen II anointed Pepin, and Charlemagne and his younger brother Carloman were anointed with their father. He began issuing charters in his own name in 760.
sections.rise:
Pepin died on 24 September 768, and Charlemagne and Carloman succeeded him. They were crowned separately on 9 October, Charlemagne at Noyon and Carloman at Soissons, and kept separate palaces while being considered joint rulers of a single kingdom. They marched together against the uprising in Aquitaine, but Carloman turned back for unknown reasons and Charlemagne finished the campaign alone, capturing Duke Hunald. The episode opened a rift between the kings.

In 770 his mother Bertrada brokered a marriage alliance with the Lombard king Desiderius, whose daughter, traditionally known as Desiderata, she brought back as his bride; Pope Stephen III wrote to both kings decrying the match. Charlemagne already had a son, Pepin, born in 769 to the Frankish noblewoman Himiltrude. Carloman died suddenly on 4 December 771, leaving Charlemagne sole king. He moved at once to secure his brother's territory, and Carloman's widow Gerberga fled with her children to Desiderius. Charlemagne ended his Lombard marriage and married Hildegard, daughter of Count Gerold, a powerful magnate in Carloman's kingdom.

His first campaign as sole king, against the Saxons, destroyed the pagan Irminsul at Eresburg. When Pope Adrian I appealed for help against Desiderius, Charlemagne first offered gold and then crossed the Alps to besiege Pavia in late 773. The city surrendered by June 774. He deposed Desiderius, took the title of King of the Lombards and returned to Francia with the Lombard royal treasury.
sections.deeds:
Charlemagne's reign was a period of expansion. He fought the Saxons almost continuously for over 30 years, crossed the Pyrenees in 778, received the submission of the Duchy of Benevento, deposed his cousin Duke Tassilo and absorbed Bavaria in 788, and warred against the Avars, whose kingdom collapsed under further campaigns by his son Pepin of Italy. His son Louis captured Barcelona in 801, enlarging the Spanish March. During the wars of the 790s he established his court at Aachen, where he built a large palace with a chapel.

On Christmas Day 800, at mass in St. Peter's Basilica, Pope Leo III proclaimed him "emperor of the Romans" and crowned him; Leo had fled to him in 799 after his enemies attacked him. Charlemagne was the first reigning emperor in the west since the deposition of Romulus Augustulus in 476. Historians differ on how far he planned the coronation: Einhard writes that he would not have entered the church had he known the pope's plan, while Roger Collins and Johannes Fried hold that he had intended it since 799 or 798.

The Capitulare missorum generale of 802 required all free men to swear loyalty to him and assigned the missi dominici in pairs, a cleric and a lay aristocrat, to administer justice in defined territories. The council of Frankfurt in 794 set grain prices and reformed the coinage. He held 23 synods, required the Rule of St. Benedict in monasteries and promoted schools; scholars such as Alcuin of York and Theodulf of Orléans gathered at his court in the revival known as the Carolingian Renaissance.
sections.opponents:
The Saxons resisted longest. In 782 the Saxon magnate Widukind returned from Denmark and defeated a Frankish army; Charlemagne compelled the Saxon magnates to hand over prisoners, and the annals record that he had 4,500 of them beheaded at Verden. Fried writes that the figure may be exaggerated but that "the basic truth of the event is not in doubt"; Alessandro Barbero calls it "perhaps the greatest stain on his reputation". The Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae imposed the death penalty for pagan practices. Frankish armies carried Saxon captives into slavery, and in the 790s Charlemagne forcibly removed a large number of Saxons to Francia. Widukind accepted baptism in 785.

Within the family, the fate of Carloman's widow and sons after the capture of Verona is unknown; Fried suggests that they were forced into a monastery or that "an act of murder" smoothed Charlemagne's ascent. In 792 his son Pepin the Hunchback, sidelined from the succession, conspired with Bavarian nobles to assassinate his father and brothers; Pepin was sent to a monastery and many of the conspirators were executed. In 778 Basque forces had ambushed and defeated his army at the Battle of Roncevaux Pass.

His imperial title brought conflict with Constantinople, where Nikephoros I was unwilling to recognise it. Later judgements have differed sharply. Martin Luther criticised his apparent subjugation to the papacy, Voltaire saw him as a despotic ruler, and German historiography either emphasised Verden, with Charlemagne as the "butcher" of the Saxons, or played it down.
sections.last:
Charlemagne left Italy in the summer of 801 and never returned to Rome. From then he ruled in a more sedentary way from Aachen and rarely led armies in person. The Divisio Regnorum of 806 set the terms of his succession: his son Charles was to have Francia and Saxony, while Pepin and Louis were confirmed in their kingdoms with additional lands; the imperial title was not addressed. He campaigned in Saxony for the last time in 804, and in 810 led a force against the Danish king Gudfred, who was murdered by two of his own men before the emperor arrived; a settlement with the Danes followed in 811. Envoys of the Byzantine emperor Michael I came to Aachen and recognised him as emperor.

In 810 and 811 his sister Gisela, his daughter Rotrude and his sons Pepin the Hunchback, Pepin of Italy and Charles the Younger died, leaving the succession plan in disarray. He declared Pepin of Italy's son Bernard ruler of Italy and made Louis, his only surviving son, heir to the rest of the empire. On 11 September 813, at a large assembly at Aachen, he crowned Louis co-emperor and Bernard king.

He fell ill in the autumn of 813 and spent his last months praying, fasting and studying the gospels. He developed pleurisy, was bedridden for seven days and died on the morning of 28 January 814. His daughters and palace officials buried him that day in the chapel at Aachen. Louis arrived 30 days later and took charge of the palace and the empire. The remains were exhumed by Frederick Barbarossa in 1165 and reinterred by Frederick II in 1215.
sections.legacy:
The stability of the reign did not long outlive him. Louis faced rebellions by his own sons, and after his death the Treaty of Verdun divided the empire into West, East and Middle Francia. Carolingians ruled, with interruptions, in East Francia until 911 and in West Francia until 987. The East Frankish king Otto the Great was crowned emperor in 962, founding or re-establishing the Holy Roman Empire, which lasted until 1806. The coronation of 800 also began a centuries-long ideological conflict with Constantinople known as the problem of two emperors.

Scriptoria produced an estimated 90,000 manuscripts in the 9th century, and the Carolingian minuscule script influenced Renaissance and modern typefaces. Thomas F. X. Noble writes that the Latin Church "as a historical phenomenon" is "a Carolingian construction". Antipope Paschal III elevated Charlemagne to sainthood in 1165 at Barbarossa's urging, but the Holy See did not recognise him as a saint.

Over 1,000 legends are recorded about him, according to Matthias Becher, and the Song of Roland and other works of the Matter of France made him a leader of Christian knights against Muslims. French and German monarchs both counted him as "Charles I"; Montesquieu viewed him as the first constitutional monarch, and Napoleon and Hitler each made use of his legacy. Historiography after the Second World War has focused on him as "the father of Europe", a view first advanced by Friedrich Schlegel, and since 1949 Aachen has awarded a prize in his honour to those who promote European unity.

summary: Charlemagne (748–814), eldest son of Pepin the Short, became king of the Franks in 768, conquered the Lombard kingdom, Bavaria and Saxony, and was crowned emperor in Rome in 800. His reforms and the learning of his court outlasted his empire, which his grandsons divided, and later ages claimed him as the "father of Europe".
references: Alessandro Barbero, Charlemagne: Father of a Continent (University of California Press, 2004)
Rosamond McKitterick, Charlemagne: The Formation of a European Identity (Cambridge University Press, 2008)
Janet L. Nelson, King and Emperor: A New Life of Charlemagne (Allen Lane, 2019)
Jennifer R. Davis, Charlemagne's Practice of Empire (Cambridge University Press, 2015)
notes: Birth year: the article says 'most likely in 748', older tradition 742, Werner's annal 747; start 748 with circa true.

The article does not state the place of death in so many words; it says he was buried in the chapel at Aachen the day he died and that Louis 'arrived at Aachen 30 days after his father's death'. The died fact therefore names only the burial place.

The article names the pope who anointed Pepin in 754 as Stephen II, but later speaks of 'the agreement between Pepin and Stephen III'; the section follows the first (Stephen II). Stephen III in the rise section is the pope elected in 768, as the article has it.
'Absorbed Bavaria in 788': the article dates the invasion to 787 and the deposition of Tassilo to 'the following year'.
Collins: planned 'as early as his meeting with Leo in 799'; Fried: 'by 798 at the latest'. Compressed to 'since 799 or 798'.

The summary's 'which his grandsons divided' rests on 'After Louis' death, the empire was divided among his sons ... by the Treaty of Verdun'; the article gives no year for Verdun or for Louis's death.
'Only surviving son' (Louis) is the article's phrase, although it also mentions illegitimate sons with church careers.
The article spells one name both Arechis and Aldechis, and 'Eindhard' once; neither spelling slip is used.

Left out for space: the Spanish embassy at Paderborn in detail, Offa of Mercia and the English exiles, the filioque dispute and the council of Aachen in 809, his wives after Hildegard (Fastrada, Luitgard), his at least 20 children, his height (1.92 m measured in 1861; 1.84 m estimated in 2010), the battle for Aachen in 1944.
